# 3.4 Linear Programming

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The four parts of a linear program

**Linear programming** is a mathematical model consisting of a **linear function to
be optimised** — maximised or minimised — **and a set of inequalities representing
the restrictions on resources**.

| Part | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Objective function** | The function to be maximised or minimised. It might represent amounts of money earned or spent, goods manufactured or delivered, or any of a variety of other quantities |
| **Constraints** | The linear inequalities |
| **Feasible region** | The solution of the system of linear inequalities |

The central fact, and the reason the method works at all: **if a linear program has
a solution, it will occur at a vertex — a corner point — of the feasible region.**
If there are multiple solutions, **at least one of them will occur at a vertex**.

That is what turns an infinite search into a finite one. The feasible region
contains infinitely many points, but only its corners need to be tested.

## Method

1. **Solve the system of linear inequalities.** Determine the coordinates of the
   vertices of the feasible region — that is, solve the system of equations
   consisting of the lines whose intersection is the vertex
2. **Evaluate the objective function** to be optimised at each vertex
3. **Identify the maximum or minimum value** of the objective function

## When two vertices tie

If **two vertices of the feasible region are both solutions** to a linear program,
then **every point on the line segment connecting the two vertices is also a
solution**.

This follows from the objective function being linear: if it takes the same value
at both ends of a segment, it takes that value all along it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Linear programming** | A model consisting of a linear function to be optimised and a set of inequalities representing restrictions on resources |
| **Objective function** | The function to be maximised or minimised in a linear program |
| **Constraints** | The linear inequalities of a linear program |
| **Feasible region** | The solution of the system of linear inequalities |
| **Vertex** | A corner point of the feasible region, where a solution will occur if one exists |

# 8.2 Sine and Cosine Curves

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The three measurements of a sinusoid

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Frequency** | The number of cycles the graph completes in an interval of $2\pi$ radians |
| **Amplitude** | Half the difference between the function's maximum and minimum values |
| **Midline** | Determined by the average of the maximum and minimum values of the function |

Amplitude and midline are the two halves of the same calculation: the **half
difference** of the extremes gives the amplitude, and their **average** gives the
midline. Together they fix the vertical position and reach of the curve, which is
why 8.3 uses them as the route from a graph back to an equation.

## The four transformations

| Transformation | Form |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal dilation** | $y = \sin(bx)$ and $y = \cos(bx)$ |
| **Vertical dilation** | $y = a\sin x$ and $y = a\cos x$ |
| **Horizontal translation** | $y = \sin(x + c)$ and $y = \cos(x + c)$ |
| **Vertical translation** | $y = \sin x + d$ and $y = \cos x + d$ |

The guide also lists **reflecting a trigonometric function** as part of this
section, without giving its form.

Each constant acts on one measurement above: $b$ changes the frequency, $a$ the
amplitude, $d$ the midline, and $c$ shifts the curve horizontally without altering
any of the three.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Frequency** | The number of cycles a sinusoidal graph completes in an interval of $2\pi$ radians |
| **Amplitude** | Half the difference between a sinusoidal function's maximum and minimum values |
| **Midline** | The line determined by the average of the maximum and minimum values |
| **Horizontal dilation** | The transformation $y=\sin(bx)$ or $y=\cos(bx)$ |
| **Vertical dilation** | The transformation $y=a\sin x$ or $y=a\cos x$ |
| **Horizontal translation** | The transformation $y=\sin(x+c)$ or $y=\cos(x+c)$ |
| **Vertical translation** | The transformation $y=\sin x + d$ or $y=\cos x + d$ |

# 8.3 Modelling Periodic Behaviour

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Modelling runs in the opposite direction to 8.2: there, constants were given and
the curve followed; here the behaviour is observed and the constants must be
recovered from it.

## Recovering period and frequency

**The smallest interval of input values over which the maximum or minimum output
values start to repeat** can be used to determine or estimate the **period and
frequency** for a sinusoidal function model.

## Recovering amplitude and vertical shift

**The maximum and minimum output values** can be used to determine the
**amplitude and vertical shift** for a sinusoidal function model.

This is 8.2's amplitude and midline calculation used in reverse: the half
difference of the observed extremes gives the amplitude, and their average gives
the vertical shift.

## Choosing sine or cosine

**Flexibly select sine or cosine functions based on the situation**, making the
equation easier to calculate as well as promoting critical thinking.

The two curves differ only by a horizontal translation, so either can model the
same behaviour — but one will usually need a smaller phase shift than the other,
and that is the one worth choosing.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Period** | Determined from the smallest interval of input values over which the maximum or minimum output values start to repeat |
| **Vertical shift** | Determined, with the amplitude, from the maximum and minimum output values |

# 10.4 Solving Trigonometric Equations and Inequalities

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The guide carries the syllabus's own sub-codes here, which are given alongside each
statement below.

## Equations

**Equivalent trigonometric forms may be useful in solving trigonometric
equations.**

**Because trigonometric functions are periodic, there are often infinitely many
solutions to trigonometric equations** (10.4.A.3). This is the fact everything else
in the section responds to — every method below is a way of cutting an infinite
solution set down to the ones being asked for.

**Algebraic and graphical methods are used to solve trigonometric equations in a
finite interval, including the use of trigonometric identities and factorisation**
(10.4.A.4).

**Inverse trigonometric functions are useful in solving equations involving
trigonometric functions, but solutions may need to be modified due to domain
restrictions.** An inverse returns one value where the equation has infinitely
many, so the others must be recovered by hand.

**In trigonometric equations arising from a contextual scenario, there is often a
domain restriction that can be implied from the context, which limits the number of
solutions** (10.4.A.6).

## Inequalities

The same three points carry over.

**Equivalent trigonometric forms may be useful in solving trigonometric
inequalities.**

**Inverse trigonometric functions are useful in solving inequalities involving
trigonometric functions, but solutions may need to be modified due to domain
restrictions** (10.4.B.2).

**In trigonometric inequalities arising from a contextual scenario, there is often a
domain restriction that can be implied from the context, which limits the number of
solutions** (10.4.B.3).

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Equivalent trigonometric forms** | Rewritings of an expression that may make an equation or inequality solvable |
| **Domain restriction** | A limit on the input values, either from an inverse function or implied by the context, which reduces the number of solutions |

# 11.1 Polar Coordinates and Graphs

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The polar coordinate system

The **polar coordinate system** is an alternative to the Cartesian system of
rectangular coordinates for locating points in a plane.

The polar coordinates of a point $P$ consist of an **ordered pair** $(r,\theta)$:

- $r$ is the **directed distance from the pole** to $P$
- $\theta$ is the **measure of the angle from the polar axis to** $OP$

The polar coordinates of the pole $O$ are $(0,\theta)$ — the distance is zero
whatever the angle, so the pole has infinitely many representations.

The angle $\theta$ can be measured in **degrees or radians**, and **both $r$ and
$\theta$ can be either positive or negative**. That last point is what the two
rules below exist to settle.

## The sign of the angle

| Sign of $\theta$ | How the polar angle is obtained |
|---|---|
| **Positive** | Rotating $OP$ **counterclockwise** from the polar axis |
| **Negative** | Rotating $OP$ **clockwise** from the polar axis |

## The sign of the distance

| Sign of $r$ | Where the polar distance is measured |
|---|---|
| **Positive** | From $O$ **along the terminal side** of the angle $\theta$ |
| **Negative** | From $O$ **on the ray opposite** the terminal side of the angle $\theta$ |

A negative $r$ therefore places the point on the far side of the pole from where
the angle points — which is why the same point has more than one set of polar
coordinates.

## Naming the plane

A plane is called an **$r\theta$-plane** when polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$ are
used to identify its points.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Polar coordinate system** | An alternative to the Cartesian system for locating points in a plane |
| **Polar coordinates** | The ordered pair $(r,\theta)$ giving a point's directed distance from the pole and the angle from the polar axis |
| **Pole** | The origin $O$ of the polar system, with coordinates $(0,\theta)$ |
| **Polar axis** | The reference ray from which the angle $\theta$ is measured |
| **Terminal side** | The side of the angle along which a positive polar distance is measured |
| **$r\theta$-plane** | A plane whose points are identified by polar coordinates |

# S1M-1 Chapter 1 - Linear and Quadratic Functions

## Chapter 1 - Linear and Quadratic Functions

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Pre-calculus AP review guide (PA). Writers: Justin Lee 10-4. Editor: Calvin 10-9. Range: Ch 1-4. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**1.2 Slopes of Lines & 1.3 Finding Equations of Line & 1.4 Linear Functions and Models**

Slope: $\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}=\frac{y2-y1}{x2-x1}$ (Linear functions have constant rate of change)

Parallel Lines: the slopes of two lines are equal

Perpendicular Lines: the slopes of two lines are negative reciprocals

Different forms of Lines

- Slope-intercept form: $y=mx+k$
- General form: $Ax+By=C$
- Point-slope form: $y-y1=m(x-x1)$
- Intercept form: $\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=1$

## 1.5 The Complex Numbers

The imaginary unit: $i=\surd -1$

Complex number: $a+bi$ (a: real part; b: imaginary part)

Complex conjugates: $z=a+bi$ and $z̄=a-bi$

$${i}^{1}=i, {i}^{2}=-1, {i}^{3}=-i, {i}^{4}=1$$

$${i}^{4n+1}=i, {i}^{4n+2}=-1, {i}^{4n+3}=-i, {i}^{4n+4}=1$$

## 1.6 Solving Quadratic Equations & 1.7 Quadratic Functions and Their Graphs

Quadratic Equation

- Standard form: $a{x}^{2}+bx+c=0, a\ne 0 \text{ and } a,b,c\in \mathbb{R}$

Method for solving quadratic equations:

- Factoring
  - Only works when the equation has rational roots
- Completing the square
  - Use when the equation has the form ${x}^{2}+(\text{ even } \text{ number })x+\text{ constant }=0$
- Quadratic formula
  - $x=\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}$

Discriminant: $D={b}^{2}-4ac$

- If D>0, the equation has 2 real solutions
- If D=0, the equation has one real solution
- If D<0, the equation has no real solutions

**ALWAYS CHECK for losing/gaining a root**

- Losing a root; eg: solve (2x-5)(x+6) = 7(x+6)
- Gaining a root; eg: solve √(3x+6)=2x+1

Quadratic Function ($f(x)=a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ or $f(x)=a(x-ℎ{)}^{2}+k$)

- Axis of symmetry: $-\frac{b}{2a}$
- Vertex: $(-\frac{b}{2a},c-\frac{{b}^{2}}{4a})$
- Opening: if a>0, the vertex is the function’s minimum; if a<0, the vertex is the function’s maximum

Average rate of change between two points of a quadratic function is equivalent to finding the slope of the secant between those points

- The instantaneous rate of change at a point can be approximated by the average rates of change of the function over small intervals containing that point

Slope and concavity:

- Slope sign → tells you if the function is going up or down
- Concavity → tells you which way the curve bends (up = ∪, down = ∩)
- Positive rate of change→graph is increasing
- Increasing rate of change→concave up
- Decreasing rate of change→concave down

**given a data chart, it is quadratic if and only if the second differences (the differences of consecutive average rates of change) are constant**

# S1M-2 Chapter 2 - Polynomial Functions

## Chapter 2 - Polynomial Functions

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Pre-calculus AP review guide (PA). Writers: Justin Lee 10-4. Editor: Calvin 10-9. Range: Ch 1-4. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 2.1 Polynomials

Polynomial function of degree n: $f(x)={a}_{n}{x}^{n}+{a}_{n-1}{x}^{n-1}+{a}_{n-2}{x}^{n-2}+…+{a}_{1}x+{a}_{0}$

- aₙ, aₙ₋₁, aₙ₋₂, …, a₀ are real numbers (n is a nonnegative integer, aₙ ≠ 0)
- The degree of a polynomial is the degree of the term of highest degree
- Leading Term: the term containing the highest power of x
- Leading coefficient: coefficient of the leading term

Degree

Name

Example

## 0

constant

f(x)=2

## 1

linear

f(x)=x

## 2

quadratic

f(x)=x^2

## 3

cubic

f(x)=x^3

## 4

quartic

f(x)=x^4

## 5

quintic

f(x)=x^5

## 2.2 Long Division; The Remainder & Factor Theorems

Example of long division:

Dividend: $2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-6x-8$; Divisor: $x-2$; Quotient: $2{x}^{2}+5x+4$ ; Remainder: 0

Dividing a polynomial with a divisor of degree n always produces a remainder whose degree is at most n-1

- Remainder Theorem: When polynomial P(x) is divided by x-a, the remainder is P(a)
- Factor Theorem: A number a is a solution of the polynomial equation f(x)=0 if and only if x-a is a factor of f(x)

## 2.3 Graphing Polynomial Functions

Fundamental shapes of polynomial functions:

**Steps to Graphing Polynomial Functions**

1. Determine the end behavior — look at the leading term ${a}_{n}{x}^{n}$: if $n$ is even and ${a}_{n}>0$, both ends go up; even and ${a}_{n}<0$, both ends go down; odd and ${a}_{n}>0$, left down/right up; odd and ${a}_{n}<0$, left up/right down.

- Use limit notation to describe end behavior: eg: $\lim_{x\to \infty }f(x)=\infty$

2. Find the y-intercept— set $x=0$ and evaluate $f(0)$; plot the point $(0,f(0))$.

3. Find the x-intercepts (zeros) — set $f(x)=0$ and solve (factor, use the quadratic formula, etc.); plot each real root on the x-axis.

4. Determine multiplicity at each zero — if the factor $(x-r{)}^{m}$: odd $m$ → graph crosses the axis; even $m$ → graph touches and turns around; larger $m$ → flatter near the root.

5. Find turning points — a polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n-1$ turning points

6. Make a sign table / test intervals — pick test points between the zeros to determine whether the graph is above or below the x-axis in each interval.

7. Sketch the curve — connect the points smoothly, respecting end behavior, intercepts, multiplicity, and turning points (no sharp corners).

8. Label key features — mark intercepts, turning points, and note the end behavior arrows.

**Important Theorems/Principles**

**Local Extrema Theorem**: a polynomial function of degree n has at most n-1 relative extrema

**Extreme Value Theorem**: if a polynomial function f is continuous on a closed interval [a,b], then f has both a maximum and a minimum value on [a,b]

**Intermediate Value Theorem**: if P(x) is a polynomial function such that a<b and P(a)≠P(b), then P(x) takes on every value between P(a) and P(b) in the interval [a,b]

**Location Principle**: if P(x) is a polynomial function with real coefficients, and a and b are real numbers such that P(a) is positive and P(b) is negative, then P(x) has at least one zero between a and b

**Rational Root Theorem**: if qx-p is a factor of a polynomial, then q must divide the leading coefficient, and p must divide the constant term

**The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra**: if P(x) is a polynomial of degree n, then the equation of P(x) has exactly n roots, including complex solutions (provided a double root is counted as 2 roots, a triple root is counted as 3 roots, and so on)

**Complex Conjugates Theorem**: if P(x) is a polynomial with real coefficients, and a+bi is an imaginary root of the equation P(x)=0, then a-bi is also a root

**Theorem 3**: suppose P(x) is a polynomial with rational coefficients, and a and b are rational numbers such that √b is irrational; if a+√b is a root of the equation P(x)=0, then a-√b is also a root

**Theorem 4**: if P(x) is a polynomial of odd degree with real coefficients, then the equation P(x)=0 has at least one real root

# S1M-4 Chapter 4 - Functions

## Chapter 4 - Functions

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Pre-calculus AP review guide (PA). Writers: Justin Lee 10-4. Editor: Calvin 10-9. Range: Ch 1-4. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 4.1 Functions

Function: a correspondence or rule that assigns to every element in a set D exactly one element in a set R

- It is a subset of the more general class of correspondences called relations
  - Relation: any correspondence/rule that pairs the members of two sets
  - ${y}^{2}=4x$ is a relation but not a function
  - The **vertical-line test**: if no vertical line intersects a given graph in more than one point, then the graph is a graph of a function

Domain: the set of x-coordinates of points on the graph

Range: the set of y-coordinates of points of the graph

Zeros: the x-intercepts of the graph

Special Functions:

- Greatest integer function (floor function)
- Its output is the greatest integer less than or equal to the number
- Notation: y=⌊x⌋
- Least integer function (ceiling function)
- Its output is the least integer greater than or equal to the number
- Notation: y=⌈x⌉
- Equal functions
- Two functions f and g are equal functions if
  - The domains of the two functions are equal
  - For all x in the domain, f(x)=g(x)

## 4.2 Operations on Functions

**the DOMAIN of each resulting function consists of those values of x common to the domains of f and g**

Composite Functions: the combination of functions in which functions are successively applied in a specific order

- $f∘g$ or $f(g(x))$is the operation of applying g and then f
- The input x must be in the domain of the inner function, AND the inner function's output must be in the domain of the outer function.

## 4.3 Reflecting graphs; Symmetry

Reflection: reflection in line t is the congruent graph symmetric to the original graph with respect to t; it is the mirror image of the graph where line t is the mirror of the reflection

- Reflection in the x-axis: y=f(x) → y=-f(x)
- Reflection in the y-axis: y=f(x) → y=f(-x)
- Reflection in the line y=x: equivalent to interchanging x and y in the equation
  - Eg: $y=3x+2$ → $x=3y+2$ → $y=\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{2}{3}$

Symmetry:

- A line $l$ is called an axis of symmetry if it is possible to pair the points of the graph in such a way that $l$ is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining each pair
- A point $O$ is called a point of symmetry of a graph if it is possible to pair the points of the graph in such a way that $O$ is the midpoint of the segment joining each pair

Tests for the symmetry of a graph:

- X-axis: replace (x,y) by (x,-y)
- Y-axis: replace (x,y) by (-x,y)
- y=x: replace (x,y) by (y,x)
- Origin: replace (x,y) by (-x,-y)

Even function: function that satisfies f(-x)=f(x) x$\in$D

Odd function: function that satisfies f(-x)=-f(x) x$\in$D

In a given interval:

Increasing: x1>x2, f(x1)≥f(x2)

Decreasing: x1>x2, f(x1)≤f(x2)

Strictly Increasing: x1>x2, f(x1)>f(x2)

Strictly Decreasing: x1>x2, f(x1)<f(x2)

## 4.4 Periodic Functions; Stretching and Translating

Periodic Functions

- A function f is periodic if there is a positive number p, called a period of f, such that f(x+p)=f(x) for all x in the domain of f
- Fundamental period: the smallest period of a periodic function
- If a periodic function has maximum value M and minimum value m, the amplitude of the function is given by ½(M-m)

Stretching and Shrinking Graphs

- Vertical stretching/shrinking of a graph can be expressed by y=cf(x) where c is positive
  - If c>1 → vertical stretch
  - If 0<c<1 → vertical shrink
  - The amplitude of the function changes to $cA$
- Horizontal stretching/shrinking of a graph can be expressed by y=f(cx) where c is positive
  - If c>1 → horizontal shrink
  - If 0<c<1 → horizontal stretch
  - The period of the function changes to $\frac{p}{c}$

Translating Graphs

- The graph of y-k=f(x-h) is obtained by translating the graph of y=f(x) horizontally h units and vertically k units

## 4.5 Inverse Functions

Inverse Function: two functions whose composition give the identity function h(x)=x

A function f has an inverse function g if and only if

- f(g(x))=x for all x in the domain of g(x) **and**
- g(f(x))=x for all the x in the domain of f(x)

Notation: inverse function of $f$ is denoted as ${f}^{-1}$ (NOTE: ${f}^{-1}$ does not mean the reciprocal of f)

If f and g are inverse functions, they are symmetric with respect to the line y=x, **so you can find the inverse function by simply switching y and x and solving for y**

Horizontal-Line test: if the graph of function y=f(x) is such that no horizontal line intersects the graph in more than one point, then f is one-to-one and has an inverse function

## 4.8 Radical Functions

Definition: A radical function is a function in which the variable appears inside a radical (root) symbol — most commonly a square root.

General form: $f(x) = \sqrt[n]{g(x)}$ where g ( x ) is some expression involving x and n ≥ 2 is an integer

Domain Rule:

- Even index (n is even): solve g ( x ) ≥ 0
- Odd index (n is odd): domain is all real numbers (unless g ( x ) itself has restrictions)

Graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$

Partial fraction: $\frac{2}{x-3}+\frac{5}{x+1}$ (Single fraction: $\frac{7x-13}{{x}^{2}-2x-3}$)

Steps to decompose a fraction with denominators that can be factored into linear factors and the degree of the numerator is less than the degree of the denominator

- Factor the denominator
- Express two fractions using A and B for the numerators
- Multiply by the least common denominator
- Solve for A and B
- Express with partial fractions

Rational Function: eg:$\frac{2{x}^{2}+3x+2}{3{x}^{2}+3x+1}$

Limit of a function: $\lim_{x\to c}f(x)=L$

- This means that when x is getting closer to c, f(x) approaches a fixed number L

Left-hand limit: x approaches c from the left $\lim_{x\to {c}^{-}}f(x)$

Right-hand limit: x approaches c from the right $\lim_{x\to {c}^{+}}f(x)$

Continuity

- A function f (x) is continuous at a point x = a if all three of the following conditions hold:
- f (a) is defined
- $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ exists
- $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a)$

A function is continuous at a point if you can draw the graph through that point without lifting your pencil, meaning that there are no holes, jumps, or vertical asymptotes

- 3 basic kinds of discontinuity at a point
- Point
- Jump
- Infinite

Horizontal asymptote

- if$\lim_{x\to \pm \infty }f(x)=b$ then line y=b is a horizontal asymptote of f(x)

Vertical asymptote

- if$\lim_{x\to {a}^{\pm }}f(x)=\pm \infty$ then line x=a is a vertical asymptote of f(x)
